title: Agile & Engineering Process
tagline: The Agile Manifesto, Scrum, Kanban, sprints, CI, and code review culture — the human and process side of shipping great software.

sections.content:
Writing good code is necessary but not sufficient. Software is built by **teams**, and teams need process to coordinate, adapt, and deliver value reliably. **Agile** is a philosophy that emerged in 2001 as a reaction to heavyweight 'waterfall' processes — it prioritises people, working software, customer collaboration, and responding to change over rigid plans and documentation.

Agile is not a single methodology — it is a set of values codified in the **Agile Manifesto** with 12 supporting principles. **Scrum** and **Kanban** are two widely used frameworks that operationalise Agile values in different ways. Engineering practices like **Continuous Integration (CI)** and **code review culture** translate Agile's 'working software frequently' principle into daily habits. Understanding these practices makes you not just a better individual contributor, but a better teammate — someone who helps the whole team ship faster and more reliably.

sections.title: A Ship That Adjusts Course vs. A Train on Fixed Rails
sections.content:
Traditional waterfall development is like a trans-continental train: the route is planned in full before departure, every stop is scheduled months ahead, and changing direction requires halting, reversing, and laying new rails — expensive and disruptive. The software industry discovered that requirements change, competitors move, and the destination itself shifts. A train is the wrong metaphor.

**Agile is a ship**: you have a general direction (vision), you make short voyages (sprints or flow cycles), you check your instruments at each port (retrospectives, reviews), and you adjust the heading before the next leg. The course is never fixed for more than a few weeks. This does not mean chaos — ships have engines, navigators, and instruments. **Scrum** is the navigation protocol (who decides the route, how the crew meets). **Kanban** is the instrument panel (how work flows through the ship). **CI** is the engine room alarm system (alerts you the moment something breaks). **Code review** is the captain's second officer — a second pair of eyes before any significant manoeuvre.

**The Agile Manifesto (2001)** has four value statements: (1) *Individuals and interactions* over processes and tools. (2) *Working software* over comprehensive documentation. (3) *Customer collaboration* over contract negotiation. (4) *Responding to change* over following a plan. Note: the right-hand items are not unvalued — the left-hand items are valued *more*.

The 12 principles emphasise: frequent delivery of working software (weeks, not months); welcoming changing requirements; business people and developers working together daily; sustainable pace; technical excellence; simplicity (maximise work not done); self-organising teams.

**Scrum** operationalises Agile with defined roles, events, and artefacts. Roles: *Product Owner* (owns the backlog, prioritises), *Scrum Master* (facilitates, removes blockers), *Development Team* (self-organising, cross-functional). Events: *Sprint* (1–4 week iteration), *Sprint Planning* (select items from backlog), *Daily Standup* (15-minute sync: done yesterday / doing today / blockers), *Sprint Review* (demo to stakeholders), *Sprint Retrospective* (team reflects: what to improve). Artefacts: *Product Backlog* (ordered list of everything), *Sprint Backlog* (items selected for this sprint), *Increment* (shippable working product).

**Kanban** focuses on *flow* rather than iterations. Work items move through columns (To Do → In Progress → Review → Done). The key constraint: **WIP (Work-In-Progress) limits** cap how many items can be in each column simultaneously. Limiting WIP reduces context switching, surfaces bottlenecks, and creates pull-based flow. Kanban suits maintenance, support, and operations work where demand is continuous and unpredictable.

**Continuous Integration (CI)** is the practice of every developer merging code to the main branch at least daily, with an automated build-and-test pipeline running on every push. The rule: if the build breaks, fixing it is the team's top priority. CI eliminates 'integration hell' — the painful merging of months of diverged work. It enforces that the main branch is *always* in a releasable state.

**Code Review Culture:** every code change is reviewed by at least one teammate before merging. Benefits: catch bugs before production, share knowledge, maintain consistent standards, foster collective code ownership. Good review culture means: reviewers give specific, actionable, respectful feedback; authors do not take feedback personally; the goal is the best code for the team, not winning an argument.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.code:
# ── GitHub Actions CI pipeline ──────────────────────────────────
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main, develop]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20'
          cache: 'npm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Run linter
        run: npm run lint

      - name: Run unit tests
        run: npm test -- --coverage

      - name: Upload coverage report
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: coverage
          path: coverage/

  # Second job: only runs after build-and-test succeeds
  e2e-tests:
    needs: build-and-test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Run E2E tests
        run: npm run test:e2e
        env:
          DATABASE_URL: ${{ secrets.TEST_DATABASE_URL }}
sections.explanation: This CI pipeline runs on every push to main and every pull request. It enforces three gates in order: lint, unit tests (with coverage), and E2E tests. A red build blocks the merge. The second job (`e2e-tests`) only runs after `build-and-test` passes — this keeps E2E feedback fast and targeted.

sections.label: Concept
sections.code:
## Scrum Sprint Artefact Template

### Sprint Goal
By end of Sprint 14, customers can complete checkout with a saved payment method.

### Sprint Backlog (selected from Product Backlog)
| ID    | Story                                      | Points | Status      |
|-------|--------------------------------------------|--------|-------------|
| US-41 | User can save a card during checkout       | 5      | In Progress |
| US-42 | User can select a saved card at checkout   | 3      | To Do       |
| US-43 | Card tokenisation via Stripe               | 8      | To Do       |
| BUG-7 | Checkout fails on mobile Safari            | 2      | Done        |

### Daily Standup Format (15 min max)
- **Done yesterday:** Implemented card save API endpoint, unit tests passing
- **Doing today:** Integrating Stripe tokenisation, writing integration tests
- **Blockers:** Need Stripe test API keys from DevOps — @sarah can you action this?

## Code Review Checklist (reviewer)
- [ ] Does the code do what the PR description claims?
- [ ] Are edge cases (null, empty array, network failure) handled?
- [ ] Are there tests for the new behaviour?
- [ ] Is there any duplication that could be extracted?
- [ ] Are names clear enough that comments are unnecessary?
- [ ] Are there any security concerns (SQL injection, unvalidated input, exposed secrets)?

## Kanban WIP Limits Example
| To Do | In Progress (WIP ≤ 3) | In Review (WIP ≤ 2) | Done |
|-------|----------------------|---------------------|------|
| 8     | 3                    | 1                   | 12   |
# If In Progress hits 3, no new work starts until an item moves to In Review.
# This surfaces bottlenecks: if Review is always full, the team needs more reviewers.
sections.explanation: The Sprint Backlog links stories to a clear Sprint Goal — 'done' is defined at the goal level, not just task level. The Daily Standup format surfaces blockers explicitly. The Code Review Checklist makes review criteria objective and consistent. The Kanban WIP limit table shows how visualising the system reveals bottlenecks that would be invisible in a backlog-only view.

sections.content: **Retrospectives are the most underrated Agile ceremony.** A team that skips retros ships the same problems sprint after sprint. Run a retro every 1–2 weeks: 10 minutes of 'what went well / what to improve', pick ONE actionable improvement, assign an owner, and check it next retro. One compounding improvement per sprint adds up to a dramatically better team within six months — without any new tools or methodologies.

items: **Agile Manifesto** values individuals, working software, customer collaboration, and responding to change — not as platitudes, but as active prioritisation over their alternatives.
**Scrum** structures work into sprints with defined ceremonies (planning, standup, review, retro) and roles (PO, SM, team) — it is about cadence and feedback loops.
**Kanban** controls flow with WIP limits, making bottlenecks visible; it suits continuous work streams better than Scrum's fixed sprints.
**Continuous Integration** ensures the main branch is always releasable — every commit triggers automated build and tests; a broken build is the team's highest priority.
**Code review culture** is about shared ownership and knowledge transfer — the best teams treat reviews as collaborative improvement, not gatekeeping.

quiz.question: Which of the following is one of the four value statements in the Agile Manifesto?
options: Comprehensive documentation over working software
Contract negotiation over customer collaboration
Responding to change over following a plan
Processes and tools over individuals and interactions
quiz.explanation: The four Agile values each state a preference: Individuals over processes, Working software over documentation, Customer collaboration over contracts, Responding to change over following a plan. Option C is a direct quote from the manifesto.

quiz.question: In Scrum, who is responsible for prioritising the Product Backlog?
options: The Scrum Master
The Development Team collectively
The Product Owner
The Engineering Manager
quiz.explanation: The Product Owner owns and orders the Product Backlog, ensuring it reflects the highest-value items first. The Scrum Master facilitates process; the Development Team does the work. The PO is accountable for maximising the value of the product.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a WIP limit in Kanban?
options: To restrict the total number of tasks in the entire backlog
To cap how many items can be in a given workflow stage simultaneously, creating pull-based flow and surfacing bottlenecks
To limit the number of developers who can work on a single task
To enforce a maximum sprint velocity across all teams
quiz.explanation: WIP limits cap in-progress work per column. When a column is full, new work cannot start until something flows forward. This forces the team to focus on finishing over starting, and makes bottlenecks visible as the 'full' column builds up.

quiz.question: What is Continuous Integration (CI)?
options: Merging code to main at least daily with automated build and tests running on every push
Deploying to production on every commit automatically
Running integration tests once per sprint before the Sprint Review
A team ritual where all developers review code together on a shared screen
quiz.explanation: CI is the practice of frequent integration (daily minimum) with automated verification. It is distinct from Continuous Delivery (automated deployment pipeline) or Continuous Deployment (auto-deploy to production). The key requirement is automation on every push.

quiz.question: The Daily Standup should focus on which three questions?
options: What did I code? What will I code? How long will it take?
What did I do yesterday? What will I do today? What blockers do I have?
What is done? What is in progress? What is in the backlog?
What went well? What could improve? What action will I take?
quiz.explanation: The classic Daily Scrum focuses on: done yesterday (coordination), doing today (commitment), and blockers (impediment visibility). It is a synchronisation meeting, not a status report to management — the Scrum Master removes blockers identified here.

quiz.question: What is the Sprint Retrospective designed to achieve?
options: Review completed work with stakeholders and gather product feedback
Plan the tasks for the upcoming sprint
Reflect on the team's process and identify one concrete improvement to implement next sprint
Report sprint velocity and burndown to the product owner
quiz.explanation: The Sprint Retrospective is an internal team ceremony (no stakeholders) focused on process improvement — not product. Teams discuss what went well, what to improve, and pick one actionable change. The Sprint Review is where stakeholders see the increment.

quiz.question: In a code review, a reviewer comments: 'This function does too many things — consider extracting the validation logic.' What kind of feedback is this?
options: Unhelpful — too vague to act on
Specific and actionable structural feedback that improves code quality
A blocker that should prevent the PR from merging until addressed
Out of scope — reviewers should only check for bugs, not structure
quiz.explanation: This is ideal code review feedback: specific (the function), actionable (extract validation logic), and grounded in a known principle (SRP / Extract Function). Good reviews improve design, not just catch bugs — this is how teams raise their collective code quality over time.

quiz.question: Which situation is Kanban generally better suited to than Scrum?
options: A team building a major new product feature over 3 months
A team doing continuous support, bug fixes, and operations where demand is unpredictable and items vary greatly in size
A team that needs defined roles (PO, SM) to manage stakeholder expectations
A team releasing a new feature every two weeks on a fixed schedule
quiz.explanation: Kanban suits continuous flow work — support queues, ops, maintenance — where the fixed-length sprint and planning ceremony of Scrum add overhead without benefit. Scrum's cadence works better for iterative feature development with predictable demand.

quiz.question: What does 'collective code ownership' mean in Agile engineering culture?
options: All code changes must be approved by the tech lead who owns the module
Any team member can improve any part of the codebase — no single person 'owns' a file
All developers are assigned specific modules they are solely responsible for
Ownership means the original author must review and merge all changes to their code
quiz.explanation: Collective ownership means anyone on the team can and should improve any part of the codebase. This removes silos, spreads knowledge, and prevents single points of failure ('only Alice understands the payment module'). Code reviews spread that knowledge actively.

quiz.question: A CI pipeline fails when a developer pushes code. According to CI best practices, what should happen next?
options: The developer should revert their commit immediately
The team should disable the failing test temporarily until the next sprint
Fixing the build becomes the team's top priority — the main branch must be green
The CI system should retry automatically three times before alerting anyone
quiz.explanation: The core CI discipline: a broken build is the team's highest priority because it blocks everyone who needs to integrate with main. The developer who broke it — with team help if needed — fixes it immediately. Disabling tests or retrying without fixing undermines the entire CI value.
